# Data and measurement

The unit of observation is an economy at a World Bank Enterprise Survey wave.
FIN14 measures the share of eligible firms with a bank loan or line of credit.
The underlying question covers a loan or credit line from a financial
institution. National rows require all six demographic and combined
breakdown dimensions to be total. Indicators join on economy and survey year.

```{r data-tables}
show <- function(x, caption = NULL, digits = 2) {
  if ("p" %in% names(x)) {
    x$p <- format.pval(x$p, digits = max(3, digits), eps = .Machine$double.eps)
  }
  knitr::kable(x, caption = caption, digits = digits, row.names = FALSE,
               booktabs = TRUE)
}
show(coverage, "Economy coverage under the alternative rules")
```

The latest FIN14-observed wave and the latest wave in the union of archived
WB_ES indicators differ for `r nrow(wave_disagreements)` economies. The
union uses rows in this snapshot, so the check covers its published vintage.

```{r survey-years}
show(pitch_years, "Survey vintage in the pitch and the rebuilt sample")
```

## Reconciliation with the visual abstract

```{r pitch-statistics}
show(cbind(Indicator = rownames(pitch_summary), pitch_summary),
     "Same-wave pitch variables, with the original units and dummy coding")
```

```{r rounding-differences}
show(pitch_differences, "Differences at displayed precision", digits = 5)
```

Both displayed differences are reproducible by rounding first to two decimal
places and then to one. The original rounding procedure is undocumented.
FIN11 includes a tiny floating-point overshoot at the upper endpoint.

## Indicator direction and sample selection

WBES documents BREADY\_DISP3 as weighted disagreement about court
independence and impartiality, following its September 2025 scale revision.
CRIME9 and BREADY\_DISP6 increase with perceived severity of a court obstacle.
The latter scores all response levels. See the
[WBES indicator guide](https://www.enterprisesurveys.org/content/dam/enterprisesurveys/documents/methodology/Indicator-Description.pdf).

```{r direction-and-selection}
show(direction_values, "Same-wave checks for court doubt")
```

The archived minimum and maximum occur in `r paste(subset(direction_values, BREADY_DISP3 == min(study$BREADY_DISP3))$economy, collapse = ", ")`
and `r paste(subset(direction_values, BREADY_DISP3 == max(study$BREADY_DISP3))$economy, collapse = ", ")`.
The pitch note cited Germany and Pakistan as the extremes.

```{r direction-correlations}
show(cbind(Indicator = rownames(direction_cor), as.data.frame(direction_cor)),
     "Correlations of the orientation checks")
```

```{r selection}
show(profiles, "Observed credit and vintage by inclusion status")
```

```{r regions}
show(region_counts, "Coverage by World Bank region")
```

EAS is East Asia and Pacific, ECS Europe and Central Asia, LCN Latin America
and the Caribbean, MEA Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan,
NAC North America, SAS South Asia, and SSF Sub-Saharan Africa.

The archived QoG variable is from La Porta et al. (1999). Code 1 is English
common law, codes 2, 4 and 5 are French, German and Scandinavian
commercial-code origins, and code 3 is Socialist. Missing codes remain
missing in the primary origin comparisons. The all-known contrast pools
codes 2 through 5. The named civil-code contrast uses codes 2, 4 and 5
as the comparison group. The generated origin audit distinguishes absent
economy rows from matched rows lacking a code and lists the pitch and sensitivity
classification. See the [QoG codebook](https://datafinder.qog.gu.se/variable/lp_legor).

```{r origin-counts}
show(origin_counts, "Archived legal-origin coverage")
```

GRAFT3 covers six public transaction types and treats refusals as affirmative
responses. DISP2 is conditional on reporting a dispute. FIN11 describes the
latest loan or line among borrowing firms. FIN20 records non-application
attributed to sufficient funds in the last fiscal year.

\newpage

# Model and hypotheses

The simple population regression function is $E[Y_i\mid D_i]=\alpha+\beta D_i$.
The extended working model is
$Y_i=\alpha+\beta D_i+\gamma B_i+\theta\log(W_i)+\delta L_i+u_i$.
$Y_i$ is FIN14 in percentage points; $D_i$ is court doubt on its published
0--100 scale, $B_i$ is the bribery incidence percentage, $W_i$ is the mean
permanent full-time-equivalent employment per firm, and $L_i$ is one for
English legal origin and zero for the model's documented comparison group.
The multivariate core first omits $L_i$ to retain all recent economies.

The disturbance represents unobserved credit demand, income, banking and
other economy conditions and survey measurement error. OLS minimizes
the sum of squared residuals with equal weight per economy. For the
classical linear model, the parameters enter linearly, the design has full
rank, the errors have conditional mean zero, and conditional error variance
is constant with zero covariance across economies. Conditional normality
additionally gives exact finite-sample classical tests. We estimate the best
linear projection as an association. Population orthogonality of projection
errors is weaker than conditional mean independence and does not identify a
causal coefficient.

Test $H_0:\beta=0$, $H_0:\gamma=0$, and $H_0:\delta=0$ against two-sided
alternatives. Greater doubt and bribery are expected to be negatively
associated with credit. A positive common-law coefficient is a literature
hypothesis. The overall joint test restricts all slopes to zero. The
institutional test restricts the included court-doubt, bribery and
legal-origin slopes jointly. For the main comparison,
$H_0:s_D\beta-s_B\gamma=0$ versus a nonzero difference. The two sample
SDs are held fixed in inference.

FIN11 conditions on observed borrowers, FIN20 may reflect equilibrium
credit demand, and DISP1 and DISP2 capture dispute incidence and selected
use of resolution. CRIME9 is an alternative perception measure. Adding
these variables tests specification sensitivity. The added fit can reflect
joint determination or selection, and national income remains unobserved.

## Fit and coefficient tests

```{r model-fit}
show(setNames(model_fit, c("Model", "N", "Slopes", "R squared", "Adjusted", "Residual SD")),
     "OLS fit and residual standard deviation", digits = 3)
```

$R^2$ is the fraction of observed between-economy variation in FIN14 explained
in sample. Adjusted $R^2$ penalizes added slopes. Changes across different
samples also reflect the change in economies. The simple and core models use
the same economies, as do the core on the QoG sample, QoG origin and full
specification. Each institutional coefficient is a conditional association
holding the other included variables fixed.

\newpage

```{r main-coefficients}
coefficient_labels <- c("(Intercept)" = "Intercept", BREADY_DISP3 = "Court doubt",
                        GRAFT3 = "Bribery", log_workers = "Log workers", common = "Common law")
display_coefficients <- subset(model_coefficients,
  (Model %in% c("Simple", "Core", "QoG origin") |
     Model == "English vs civil codes" & Term == "common") & Inference == "HC3",
  select = -Inference)
display_coefficients$Term <- unname(coefficient_labels[display_coefficients$Term])
show(display_coefficients,
     "Primary coefficients with HC3 standard errors and 95 percent intervals", digits = 4)
```

The simple court slope explains little variation. Adding bribery and size
improves fit on the same economies. The negative bribery slope remains
visible on the smaller legal-origin sample. Both origin intervals admit
negative and positive conditional associations.

HC3 adjusts uncertainty for uneven residual variance and leverage. The
reported t and robust Wald F reference distributions use the OLS residual
degrees of freedom as a finite-sample approximation. The conventional
inference and full coefficients are in the generated model tables.

```{r model-joints}
show(subset(joint_results, Model %in% c("Core", "QoG origin")),
     "Classical and HC3 joint tests", digits = 4)
```

\newpage

## Effects in interpretable units

```{r translated-effects}
show(core_effects, "Core associations in FIN14 percentage points, with HC3 intervals", digits = 3)
```

```{r partial-fit}
show(partial_fit, "Sample standard deviations and partial R-squared", digits = 4)
```

The core bribery estimate corresponds to about
`r round(abs(core_effects$Estimate[2]), 1)` percentage points lower credit
holding for a ten-point rise in the incidence of bribe requests. The
court-doubt interval spans zero for an equally sized change. Partial
$R^2$ measures the fraction of residual variation in the model
omitting the given term that is accounted for when it is added. The signed
contrast uses both HC3 variances and their covariance. An exploratory
intersection-union test asks if the standardized bribery slope is negative
and exceeds court doubt in absolute magnitude. Its one-sided tests require
the court-minus-bribery contrast to be positive and the court-plus-bribery
contrast negative. The larger component p-value is
`r format.pval(bribe_magnitude_p, digits = 3)`. The economic
comparisons refer to the average economy association and describe credit
holding, which combines demand and lending decisions.

\newpage

# Diagnostics and remedies

## Error variance and robust inference

The studentized Breusch--Pagan test regresses squared residuals on the
original design and tests constant conditional error variance against a
variance relationship with the regressors. The statistic is $nR^2$ of the
auxiliary regression. Survey precision and cross-economy variation motivate
HC3 even when this test is weak. Heteroskedasticity affects classical
standard errors and efficiency. HC3 re-estimates the covariance of the OLS
fit, so the OLS slopes remain the same. Comparable indicator-level survey
variances are unavailable in these CSVs.

```{r bp-and-se}
show(setNames(bp, c("Model", "Chi squared", "df", "p")),
     "Studentized Breusch-Pagan tests", digits = 3)

display_se <- se_comparison
display_se$Term <- unname(coefficient_labels[display_se$Term])
for (column in c("Classical_p", "HC3_p")) {
  display_se[[column]] <- format.pval(display_se[[column]], digits = 3)
}
names(display_se) <- c("Model", "Term", "Estimate", "Classical SE", "HC3 SE",
                       "Classical p", "HC3 p")
show(display_se, "Conventional and HC3 inference on the same OLS coefficients", digits = 3)
```

The core and the origin tests show little evidence of the specified
variance relationship. The full specification is close to the conventional
5 percent threshold. HC3 changes the reported precision without changing
the conclusions for court doubt, bribery or legal origin.

## Residual ordering

Durbin--Watson is the squared change between neighboring residuals divided
by the sum of squared residuals. The formal reference tests zero
first-order dependence against either sign along each imposed sequence,
simulating normal homoskedastic independent errors with the design fixed.
The p-values are conditional on those assumptions. In a country
cross-section, neighbors in a sorted list lack a temporal interpretation.
A random reordering of the same core residuals gives a middle 95 percent
range of `r sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", random_dw[1], random_dw[2])`. Shared shocks
within geographical regions are a more plausible dependence concern.

```{r dw-checks}
show(dw, "Durbin-Watson under three orderings", digits = 3)
```

The nominal core p-value is smaller when ordering by survey year. The
ordering places distinct economies with similar vintages next to each
other and sometimes changes the conclusion of the reference test.

\newpage

## Collinearity and functional form

VIF compares coefficient variance with that under an orthogonal design
at equal regressor and disturbance variances. It measures precision loss.
On the QoG sample, court doubt and the severe-obstacle share correlate
at `r round(court_correlations["BREADY_DISP3", "CRIME9"], 2)`. The core retains
court doubt as the direct measure of the proposed perception channel.
The full-model maximum VIF is `r round(max(subset(vifs, Model == "Full pitch terms")$VIF), 2)`.
The model choice follows the distinct survey concepts and denominators.

```{r vifs}
vif_wide <- reshape(vifs, idvar = "Term", timevar = "Model", direction = "wide")
names(vif_wide) <- c("Term", "Core", "QoG", "Full pitch")
show(vif_wide, "Variance inflation factors by model")
```

```{r court-correlations}
court_terms <- c("BREADY_DISP3", "CRIME9", "DISP2")
show(cbind(Measure = court_terms, as.data.frame(court_correlations[court_terms, court_terms])),
     "Pairwise court correlations on the full-model sample")
```

```{r form}
show(setNames(form_checks, c("Model", "Min fitted", "Max fitted", "Outside 0-100",
                             "F", "df1", "df2", "p")),
     "Fitted range and HC3 RESET-style test of added fitted powers", digits = 4)
```

The RESET-style check tests the joint restriction that adding squared and
cubed standardized fitted values contributes nothing to the conditional
mean. A rejection can reflect omitted variables or misspecified functional
form. The core has an out-of-range fitted value. The fractional response
sensitivity enforces the bounds.

\newpage

## Residuals and influence

```{r residual-plots, fig.width=8, fig.height=3.15, out.width="100%"}
old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 0.5, 1), las = 1, family = "sans")
plot(core_diagnostics$Fitted, core_diagnostics$Residual, pch = 16, cex = 0.55,
     col = "#24536B", xlab = "Fitted credit share", ylab = "OLS residual")
abline(h = 0, col = "grey55", lty = 2)
lines(lowess(core_diagnostics$Fitted, core_diagnostics$Residual), col = "#A4482C", lwd = 2)
plot(core_diagnostics$Leverage, core_diagnostics$Cook, pch = 16, cex = 0.55,
     col = "#24536B", xlab = "Leverage", ylab = "Cook's distance",
     ylim = c(0, 1.15 * max(core_diagnostics$Cook)))
with(head(top_core_cook, 3), text(Leverage, Cook, labels = Economy, pos = 3, cex = 0.72))
par(old_par)
```

```{r influence}
show(top_core_cook[c("Economy", "Fitted", "Residual", "Studentized", "Leverage", "Cook")],
     "The five largest core Cook's distances", digits = 3)
```

Leverage identifies unusual regressor values, while Cook's distance also
uses the residual to summarize the potential effect on the fitted equation.
The influence sensitivities retain the full sample for the primary fit.
